title: Facilitating Learning — floor exercise
lead: One page. Print it, or open it on a phone. Everything the exercise needs is on it.
pointsTitle: The four points of the cycle
pointsLead: Tape a circle on the floor and mark four points on it. Choose one wall as the top. Put **Active** at the top, **Reflective** on the right, **Theorist** at the bottom and **Pragmatist** on the left: standing in the centre and facing Active, Reflective is on your right. Draw arrows round the circle in that order (Active → Reflective → Theorist → Pragmatist → Active). That is the direction the cycle runs, and it matches the picture on everyone's phone.
positions: Each result says where to stand: at one of the four points, on the circle halfway between two neighbouring points, or in the centre. Expect more than half the room to be between two points or in the centre. That is deliberate: the quiz names a single point only when the lead is clear.
promptsLead: In groups by point of the cycle, about 8 minutes each. Take one answer from each group before moving on, so no group hears only itself.
prompts: What does a session feel like when it is run entirely from your point of the cycle? Name what a participant gets from it, and name what they miss.
Think of a session where you were the one out of step with how it was being run. What did you do — and what could the trainer have done that would have brought you back in?
Which part of the cycle do you skip when you plan a session? What would you have to do differently, concretely, to run that part properly?
lopsidedLead: Eleven Reflectives and one Active happens, and the session as written does not handle it. The imbalance is not a problem with the exercise — it is the most interesting thing in the room, provided you say so.
lopsided: **Never leave one person standing alone.** Ask them to join the nearest group and speak as their point's delegate. Standing alone in front of a room is a different exercise from the one you meant to run.

**Say the imbalance out loud and use it.** "This room is nearly all Reflective. What does that predict about the sessions we design together this week?" That question is worth more than the original three.

**Use the people between points and in the centre.** People halfway between two points join the smaller of their two groups; people in the centre go to the smallest group. Tell them why: they are covering a gap, not being corrected.
**If a point is empty, give it to the fullest group.** Ask them to argue that point's case for five minutes. Arguing for the appetite you least share is the actual learning objective.
**Break the big group into pairs.** A group of eleven is not a discussion, it is a queue. Run the three questions in pairs inside the large group, then take one answer from each pair.
**Walk the cycle.** If time allows, have each group pass one of its answers clockwise to the next point and ask that group what it would add. It shows the cycle as a sequence, not four camps.
**Do not re-run the assessment to get a better spread.** The spread is the data. Rigging it teaches the room that the instrument is a formality.
running: 0–10 min — people arrive with a result. Read out the four descriptions; ask people to stand where their result says.
10–15 min — name the shape of the room. Move the people between points and in the centre into groups.
15–40 min — the three questions in groups by point of the cycle, one answer taken from each group after each.
40–60 min — whole group: what does a trainer have to do to run all four? Collect concrete moves, not principles.
60–90 min — the rest of the session as planned.
sayThis: This is a preference, not a diagnosis, and the research does not support teaching people according to a measured style. We are standing round the cycle so that you can see the room contains all four, not so that you can be told how you learn.
caution: If someone says the result is wrong about them, they are right and you should say so. The instrument has never been validated. What it can do is start the argument — an argument about what a session misses when a trainer runs only their own quarter of the cycle.
